title: New regulations on distance learning broadly welcomed
content:
Tweet
Brazil’s new regulatory framework for distance learning has been broadly welcomed in the higher education sector.
New legislation setting out to both strengthen the quality of distance education and limit its use in certain programmes was introduced in legislation signed off in May.
It prohibits 100% remote undergraduate courses and ensures that only 30% of the workload of in-person programmes can now include distance learning activities.
The legislation represents a response to concerns about the huge rise in remote learning over the past decade and the impact on the quality of higher education provision.
According to the Ministry of Education, the changes introduced in the decree seek to boost the quality of distance learning in Brazilian higher education while recognising it as a strategic tool for education expansion and access.
Minister of Education Camilo Santana, speaking at the signing ceremony, said: “We believe that distance learning can provide students with an experience as rich as that of other programmes, as long as there is an effective commitment from everyone to the teaching and learning process.”
Claudia Costi, former senior director for global education at the World Bank, said the measures are “positive, even if overdue”.
“Distance learning is certainly a way to expand access to higher education – this has been the case in other countries – but it must be quality education. There’s no point in reaching remote areas if the education offered is poor,” she said, as reported by Valor International.
Costin noted that one in two students drop out of distance learning programmes and poor course quality is a key reason.
The Foundation for the Center for Science and Distance Higher Education of the State of Rio de Janeiro (Cecierj Foundation) told CNN Brazil that the new guidelines will have a positive impact on distance learning and defends this model as an important tool for the democratisation of access to higher education.
Threefold increase in programmes
Enrolments in distance learning programmes in Brazil have grown by 326% in 10 years, reaching 4.91 million students between 2022 and 2023 and representing almost half of the total enrolments in Brazilian higher education.
At the same time, enrolments in the in-person programmes fell by 29.1% between 2013 and 2023, according to the 15th edition of the Map of Brazilian Higher Education.
The new legislation, which was signed into law by President Luís Inácio Lula da Silva on 19 May, is the result of a dialogue across different sectors of Brazilian society about the need for a new Distance Learning Policy and will be regulated by the Ministry of Education and the National Council of Education.
Decree 12546 was drafted by a committee of experts with extensive experience in distance education and public policy.
It also involved meetings with the Advisory Council for the Improvement of Higher Education Regulation and Supervision Processes; technical visits and meetings with representative bodies, social movements, and international experts; as well as public hearings at the Education Committee of the Chamber of Deputies.
Clearer definitions set out
The new decree includes clear definitions of in-person, hybrid, and distance learning programmes.
Hybrid programmes, which are a new format, will include at least 30% in-person activities (professional internships, outreach activities, and laboratory practices), and at least 20% will involve either in-person or facilitated synchronous activities – real-time interactions with a maximum of 70 students per teacher and facilitator and controls on attendance.
Under the new rules in Brazil, distance learning programmes should comprise a minimum of 20% in-person and-or mediated synchronous activities. Each distance learning course will have to include at least one in-person test focused on analysis, synthesis, or practice, which will have the highest weighting of any single element in the final grade. Certain undergraduate programmes have been ruled incompatible with distance learning. They are medicine, law, dentistry, nursing, and psychology. Distance learning is also prohibited in medicine programmes. Other programmes in the field of health and programmes for professional training (“licenciaturas”) can only exist in in-person or hybrid formats. Higher education institutions interested in offering distance learning programmes must request a specific accreditation from the Ministry of Education. One of the new requirements for obtaining this accreditation is that the institution must have a distance learning centre, which must include resources such as internet, study spaces and laboratories (where applicable), and academic spaces that support students. They must also have facilitators – described as ‘teaching mediators’ – and tutors. Tutors must be trained in the courses they will teach. Also, facilitators must only perform administrative tasks and no teaching functions. Changes to be brought in gradually The changes outlined in the decree will be introduced gradually. According to the Ministry of Education, higher education institutions will have two years to adapt their programmes. Students enrolled in distance learning programmes with different characteristics from those covered by the decree will be able to complete their studies with no changes. Since its creation, the decree has received a lot of attention from bodies representing private higher education institutions, which account for 79.3% of total higher education enrolments in Brazil and were responsible for offering 95.9% of distance learning courses in Brazil in 2023. While the new decree imposes limits and requirements as a means to ensure quality, its implementation and how it will be monitored present significant challenges for the Brazilian government in the coming period. Janguiê Diniz, CEO of the Brazilian Association of Higher Education Providers (ABMES), highlighted the essential role that distance education plays in the democratisation of Brazilian higher education and warned of the risks that this could go backwards if the regulation is implemented without dialogue and balance. Distance learning is of paramount importance for Brazil. Many people were only able to reach higher education thanks to it,” Diniz said in a live broadcast on YouTube held a few hours after the publication of the decree. ABMES, which contributed to the formation of the new decree, also held a seminar on 10 June, titled “New distance learning milestone: perspectives, challenges, and paths”. Financial analysts present at the event warned that the decree is likely to increase operational costs for institutions, especially with the requirement for mediated synchronous activities and adaptations in distance learning centres, in addition to reducing revenues through the ending of high-margin distance learning courses such as nursing. In general, the education media agrees that the decree is positive, although some have been critical of the delays in tackling the issue and say the proposals don’t go far enough. Professor Joana Angélica Guimarães da Luz , rector of the Federal University of Southern Bahia, in an article in Folha de São Paulo, complained about a lack of debate about the use of distance learning in Brazilian public universities, which generally offer better teaching and research. She wrote: “With the current technological advances and an ever-increasing network of public universities spread throughout all regions of Brazil, the conditions are already in place for a better-founded public distance education network to exist throughout the Brazilian territory.” Increasingly popular teaching method Distance learning is an increasingly popular teaching method in other South American countries, which has both positives and negatives. On the one hand, it has the potential to expand access to higher education, and on the other, it promotes the privatisation of the system, with risks to the quality of education. Argentina and Paraguay have updated their legislation on distance learning in higher education in recent years, the former in 2023 and the latter in 2024. Both have reduced the use of distance learning as an asynchronous method but make no reference to real-time online interactions. Like Brazil, Paraguay defines some areas in which distance learning is not acceptable. These are natural sciences, engineering and technology, medical sciences and agricultural sciences.

title: Bangladeshi students reject political and media hostility
content:
Tweet
Bangladeshi students have voiced strong concerns over increasingly hostile media coverage by the right-wing press in Denmark, fuelling fears of growing ‘Muslim immigration’ at Denmark’s universities, and claims by right-wing politicians that they are exploiting loopholes in immigration law to take Danish jobs.
The Bangladesh Association of Students and Alumni (BASAD) in Denmark said it is “deeply concerned by the tone and framing” of the coverage on 24NEWS and by the Ritzau news agency of reports of increasing numbers of students coming to Denmark from Bangladesh.
“These students come to Denmark through transparent, lawful processes – meeting all academic and visa requirements, paying high tuition fees, and pursuing their studies in accordance with Danish standards.
“Their presence reflects the strength and credibility of Denmark’s education system, not a flaw in it,” BASAD told University World News.
On 9 July the newspaper Berlingske Tidende ran the headline: “Remarkable increase in students from Bangladesh: It smells like something we’ve seen before”, alluding to the influx of Nepalese students earlier this year as reported by University World News .
“It has been about two months since Minister for Immigration and Integration Kaare Dybvad Bek closed a loophole in the law that gave people from third-world countries direct access to the Danish labour market. Now it appears that a new one has opened, says the union”, the newspaper stated.
This was followed by a report in the Fagbladet 3F with the
headline : “Every sixth student at RUC university [Roskilde masters] is from Bangladesh”.
In 2024, one in six newly admitted masters students at Roskilde University (RUC) was from Bangladesh, the publication said, claiming: “It is most likely that people from Bangladesh use study stays in Denmark as a backdoor to the Danish labour market and permanent residence.”
The report said suspicion had long been simmering that Bangladeshis were gaining easy access to the Danish labour market through study stays at the country’s universities, bypassing the usual rules that regulate employment of international labour.
While nine students from Bangladesh were admitted to RUC in 2020, that number had increased to 300 in 2024 – more than 30 times more, the publication reported.
Denmark’s right-wing parties quickly responded, demanding action. The Danish People’s Party’s immigration spokesperson Mikkel Bjørn, told 24NEWS: “It is deeply serious that Islamic immigration is growing at our universities. We have seen time and time again that so-called temporary presence becomes permanent residence. It starts with a study stay – and ends with family reunification and a lifelong presence.”
On 9 July, Peter Skaarup of the right-wing populist Denmark Democrats party asked the Minister of Immigration and Integration Kaare Dybvad Bek in Parliament to comment on the Berlingske Tidende report and to explain “whether the government is ready to look at measures that close the loophole to the Danish labour market that currently exists for students from third countries on state-approved programmes”.
He demanded detailed information from the minister breaking down the number of immigrants from Bangladesh arriving in 2019-2025 on the basis of their residence category, such as asylum, employment, family reunification, study, or other.
BASAD told University World News that Bangladeshi students were being unfairly characterised as undocumented migrants when in fact they had come through legal channels. “It is especially disappointing to see narratives that misrepresent this community. These students are not exploiting the system – they are fully engaged in it: paying tuition, following legal requirements, and contributing academically and economically,” it said. It was important to highlight that access to the labour market is a standard feature of international student policies globally, BASAD said. “In countries with limited scholarship opportunities, part-time work is often essential not only for financial survival but also for integration and professional growth. This is not a loophole – it is a natural and expected part of the international education experience,” BASAD noted. Some Bangladeshi students have been documenting their compatriots’ study experience in Denmark as part of their research. At Aalborg University, Nusrat Jahan Shimul delivered her MSc in Global Refugee Studies thesis in 2024, which found that Bangladeshi students face unequal treatment not only in the labour market but also within their educational institutions in Denmark. “I am myself a student migrant from Bangladesh pursuing my master’s degree. During my whole study period, I have struggled a lot maintaining the balance between my study, work, and personal life. While searching for jobs, I have been discriminated against because of language and limited working hours as per my immigration rules,” Shimul stated. The Danish Development Research Network Sabbir Irfan reported last year that there had been a surge in Bangladeshi students dropping out of their programmes, which posed a significant challenge for institutions and the Danish education system. This was despite the fact that a “substantial portion” of Bangladeshi students “excel academically and pursue diverse paths post-graduation – such as returning to Bangladesh or relocating to other countries with developmental project works, or settling in Denmark for enhanced opportunities”. Susan Wright, Professor of Educational Anthropology at the Danish School of Education at Aarhus University, told University World News that Denmark is trying to re-internationalise its higher education “but limits its ambition to only attracting international students who will contribute as graduates to the Danish economy”. The viability of a university programme is thus gauged by the number of graduates employed in the Danish labour market. Wright said this poses two problems. First, she said, many Danish as well as international students take courses with the aim of contributing to social and economic development elsewhere in the world, not just in Denmark. “These students might be employed in their home country or in global companies, NGOs, or international organisations and be ambassadors for Denmark and its education. But they do not ‘count’ in the statistics on graduate employment for their university programme, and their absence from the Danish labour market may well undermine the viability of that programme.” Second, as the Bangladeshi Students’ Association makes clear and as is also reflected in research at the Centre for Higher Education Futures , she said that international students face great difficulties in obtaining student jobs, let alone employment after graduation, that relate to their studies and help them build a career in Denmark. She added that many in Denmark think that the kind of prejudice exemplified by the newspaper headlines about this case are damaging Denmark's image. Christoffer Rosenkvist, chair of the National Union of Students in Denmark, told University World News: “The increase in applications from Bangladesh is certainly significant. However, it is very important to note that, within the current Danish legal framework, it is legal for foreign non-EU students to study and work in Denmark provided all conditions here are met. “The internationalisation of our higher educational institutions is not only a huge asset for our students and educational institutions, but for Danish society as a whole,” he said. He added that, when considering solutions to the problems of employment, it is important to address both the study and work conditions of the students in question. Iris Kimizoglu, president of the European Students’ Union, told University World News, that addressing any issue concerning a minority of students misusing visas should not impact the majority of Bangladeshi students who had fulfilled all the legal requirements on entry. “We reject xenophobic and racist narratives and warn against measures that discredit and disadvantage the broad majority of honest students from Bangladesh,” she said. Dr Bernd Parusel, senior researcher in political science at the Swedish Institute for European Policy Studies and an expert on migration, told University World News that reports about international students using their residence permits or visas for reasons other than studying have also been a concern in many other European Union member countries, as a briefing from the European Migration Network showed a couple of years ago. “Governments and higher education institutions are facing a dilemma. On the one hand, they know that allowing international students to work, at least part-time, is important for many students, especially in countries where tuition fees or the cost of living are high. “If a destination country is very strict regarding students’ right to work, that makes the country less attractive as a destination for students,” he stated. “After all, many domestic students work as well. On the other hand, countries want to make sure that those that are admitted for study purposes really have studying as their main intention. Governments also want to avoid exploitation in the labour market and wage-dumping,” he added. He said that solving this dilemma by finding a reasonable middle ground between these two political goals is not easy. “If study permits are used for work purposes, including low-skilled work, that also shows that European countries have a huge demand for foreign labour,” he stated. “Officially, some EU countries only want to attract skilled workers for high-paid jobs, but our economies have a big demand for lower-skilled or unskilled workers as well. I think this needs to be acknowledged and dealt with too.”

title: Trump’s ‘Big Bill’ to cost students, universities billions
content:
Tweet
As warplanes roared overhead celebrating Independence Day on 4 July, United States President Donald J Trump signed into law a bill that dramatically downsizes the federal government’s role in financing America’s colleges and universities.
Dubbed (by Trump) the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ (OBBB, House of Representatives Bill), the budget reconciliation law alters how Pell Grants (available to the nation’s poorest students) are calculated in financial aid formulae.
It drastically reduces the amount of money students’ families can borrow for them under the federally insured student loan programme, imposes a graduate ‘earning test’ for programmes to maintain their access to federal student loans, and ends the Public Service Loan Forgiveness programme that former president Joe Biden had expanded four years ago.
The US$1 trillion cut to Medicare could result in 3.4 million college and university students losing their healthcare and the closure of rural hospitals run by universities.
The bill also increases the endowment tax for half of America’s colleges and universities.
Though the bill does not mention America’s historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs), because a disproportionate share of their students are economically disadvantaged, cuts to student aid, loans and Medicare will fall more heavily on students attending these institutions.
In total, the OBBB cuts more than a trillion dollars from the US budget over 10 years and increases the debt by US$4.2 trillion in order to pay for US$4.5 trillion in tax cuts – that will see the wealthiest 1% of American households save US$12,000 in taxes while the bill costs the poorest Americans US$1,600 a year.
Before signing the almost 900-page omnibus bill that was passed by the House of Representatives by two votes and in the Senate when Vice-President JD Vance broke a 50-50 tie, Trump called the OBBB: “The most popular bill ever signed in the history of our country.”
Three days before Trump signed the law, Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, whose department is now tasked with writing thousands of regulations required by the bill, took to X to thank Republican senators for passing the OBBB and said: “By establishing loan limits, the bill closes the spigot of federal subsidies that drive up college costs and burden families. The bill also simplifies and streamlines student loan repayment for millions of borrowers.”
Notwithstanding Trump’s comment about the OBBB’s popularity, critics of the bill, like Sameer Gadkaree , president and CEO of the Institute for College Access and Success (TICAS), who called it “one big mistake”, are more in line with public opinion.
On 18 June, Fox News, which generally supports the president, reported that a poll it had commissioned showed a 28-point gap between those who supported the OBBB and those opposed to it: 38% to 59%.
“From Congress to the White House, it’s painfully apparent that federal policy-makers are divesting from higher education access, success, and affordability,” said Gadkaree in a TICAS press release.
“This misguided direction will reverse 60 years of progress toward increased educational attainment and undermine the long-time consensus on the need to invest in a globally competitive workforce. The result will be a less prosperous nation,” he noted.
In a letter written to the leaders of the Senate a few days before the final vote, Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education (ACE), writing on behalf of 35 national organisations, including the American Association of Colleges of Nursing, the American Association of State Colleges and Universities, and the Council for Higher Education Accreditation, strongly criticised the bill.
“The totality of the funding cuts, policy changes, and tax increases will have a negative impact on the ability of current and future students to access postsecondary education and harm the ability of colleges and universities to carry out their vital education and research missions,” wrote Mitchell.
Jordan Nellums, higher education senior policy associate at the New York-based Century Foundation, a progressive think tank founded in 1919, slammed the bill, especially for how it will impact HBCUs. “The One Big Beautiful Bill represents a tremendous step backwards for investing in higher education, especially for institutions [for example, HBCUs] that have historically been underfunded and done the crucial work of educating students that come from lower- to middle-income backgrounds.” Instead of taking a scalpel to reform some of the student loan programmes to solve the student debt crisis, the bill makes tremendous cuts to these programmes. “As is often said, when higher education experiences a cold, HBCUs experience the flu because they educate higher proportions of low-income and middle-income students, and students from under-represented communities. The bill is a disaster for those institutions that are doing this crucial work,” Nellum told University World News. Pell Grant changes The OBBB changes where a recipient’s Pell Grant, which remains at US$7,395, is placed in the formula for determining student aid. Under the old system, Pell Grants were considered ‘first-dollar’ aid, meaning that they were the first monies used to determine student aid. “Then,” explained Jon Fansmith, ACE’s senior vice-president for government relations and national engagement, “you layer other forms of federal and state and institutional aid on top until you’ve covered the needs of the student. Changing how you make the calculation, especially given the ties between Pell eligibility and state aid programmes, is introducing a source of complexity and uncertainty in how we package aid.” He noted: “The motivation appears to be an idea that there are students who get all their cost of attendance covered by institutional aid, a free ride scholarship.” Under the system envisaged by the OBBB, Pell Grants will be added at the end of the calculation. Mark Salisbury, co-founder and CEO of TuitionFit, which helps students navigate the complexities of understanding the tuition and fee structures of American colleges and universities, told University World News that the number of students who will be affected by this is relatively small. “But, for those individual students, the difference could be substantial. It will be interesting to see how the institutions respond to it. It’s not crazy to think that the institutions will just say: ‘Well, I’m not making money off you anyway, so we’re not going to help’,” he noted. The OBBB provides for a US$10.5 billion top-up for the Pell Grant system, which is far short of the US$97 billion shortfall that the Congressional Budget Office estimates will accrue over the next 10 years. Loan programme caps The federally insured undergraduate loan programme, which this year allowed students to borrow up to US$23,000 over four years, remains untouched. However, the total amount of money undergraduates and their families can borrow under the federally insured programme has been dramatically reduced. The Parent Plus programme, which for decades has allowed parents to borrow an unlimited amount of money, which, as Salisbury explained, has been pointed to as one of the reasons for America’s student debt crisis, has been capped at US$20,000. Previously, if you wanted to go to a certain college where tuition and fees were US$70,000, explained Salisbury, if you received a US$10,000 scholarship, you could borrow US$5,500 from the federal government, which left US$54,500. Under the old Parent Plus programme, parents could borrow this every year for the four years, producing a debt of US$218,000. Salisbury thinks that the caps to the Parent Plus programme and GradPlus programme are a necessary corrective to what he termed “a sort of slush fund” that allowed people to borrow more than they should, which contributed to the student debt crisis, which today is US$1.6 trillion . On an ACE webinar on Thursday 10 July, Fansmith raised a number of concerns about the replacement for the GradPlus program, the Graduate Federal Loan Cap System (GFLCS), and the government’s distinctions between what are termed “graduate programmes” and “professional programmes”. The latter, he said, are what we think of as terminal degrees: PhDs, MDs, JDs, MBAs. They have different borrowing limits than do regular graduate programs: US$20,500 a year (for a maximum of US$100,000) for regular graduate programs vs US$50,000 a year (for a maximum of US$200,000). “We’re still working through what the impacts would be,” said Fansmith, “the one that’s most immediate is around the health professions. If you look at the averages for an MD programme, dental programme, or veterinary programme, both on annual and aggregate levels, on average they exceed the US$50,000 and US$200,000 level. “We have a lot of concern about what that might mean, especially in those fields where we don’t have nearly as many people entering, completing, and entering the workforce as we frankly need in this country,” he noted. Fansmith went on to say that students who require more money than they can borrow from the federal government will have to go to the private loan market. According to the Higher Education Inquirer, in 2023, the private student loan market was valued at US$412.7 billion and is expected to grow to almost a trillion dollars by 2032. Borrowing from organisations like Sallie Mae (Student Loan Marketing Association) or the Massachusetts Educational Financial Authority, a not-for-profit education lender, explained Salisbury, is different from borrowing from the federally insured student loan programme. “It’ll be much harder to do because the private lender is going to have a much more stringent set of criteria to determine whether I, as a student or parent, am in a position to be able to pay back the loan,” he said. HBCUs will be especially hard hit by the caps, said Nellums. “In 2012, the Obama administration introduced stricter credit requirements to be able to qualify for the Parent Plus Loan Program. Even with what was a minor tweak to the program, nearly 30,000 students experienced adverse credit checks. “And HBCUs lost about US$150 million, almost 20% of their total funding,” said Nellums. A 2019 study reported that parents of 19% of Black students at HBCUs took out Parent Plus loans to help pay for their children’s college education, even though they make up only 12% of the national student body. Since the chronically underfunded HBCUs do not have the resources to make up this shortfall, enrolment is likely to suffer. The replacement of the GradPlus programme by one with tighter borrowing limits will be devastating to HBCUs, he says, because nearly 40% of these loans go to students who are attending HBCUs. ‘Pie in the sky’ accountability tests Both ACE’s officials and Salisbury wondered aloud about how the ‘accountability’ mandate created by the OBBB will work. According to Fansmith, the assumption is: “If you enter a programme and you have to borrow to attend this programme, you should be earning enough money to repay your loans. You should be able to out-earn someone who doesn’t have your credential or doesn’t have a credential at your level. Under the OBBB, in order for students to be able to access federally insured student loans, programmes must demonstrate that four years after graduation, their graduates earn 50% more than workers in that state between the ages of 25 and 34 who have only a high school diploma; if most of a programme’s students come from outside the state, then the Department of Education (DoE) will use the national average of 25- to 35-year-olds who have only a high school diploma. If a programme fails to demonstrate that its graduates have this earning premium in two out of three years, then students applying to that program lose eligibility for federally insured student loans. The bar on access to federal funding lasts at least two years, and to be lifted requires that the program demonstrate its graduates have earned 50% more than those with high school diplomas. “To implement this accountability system, you’re going to need data reported by the institutions to the Department of Education. You’re going to use information from institutions or departments and individuals. “Then you’re going to have to match this data to IRS (Income Tax) data about earnings to make these comparisons. It will be very complicated.” Salisbury was more pungent, characterising this as only one instance in the bill when “the right hand did not know what the left hand was doing”. Back in February and March, said Salisbury, McMahon fired thousands of DoE researchers and cancelled “the contracts for all the third-party entities that would do a lot of the heavy lifting to process, organise, and validate the data that gets collected from colleges and universities. So the quality of the data that the federal government is going to have is really up in the air; it’s not dependable or doesn’t exist”. He added: “How in the world are you going to be able to enforce or make decisions based on the law? You’re going to need far better data than the data we actually even have right now.” When I mentioned to Salisbury that, a number of times, I’ve been told that colleges and universities themselves don’t have this data at the programme level, he wasn’t surprised. “No, they don’t have it. The way that the data has been collected has generally been for the students from a given school. “For student borrowers, the federal government has access to students’ tax returns. And so from those individuals, they’ve got data on income that they can tie back to what major that student graduated from. “So now it’s up to the school to collect that data somehow, and the school has no power to compel any of their alumni to provide that information. This is a great example of the ‘pie in the sky’ idea. But nobody ever thought about how you set up the infrastructure to get the data to be able to make the policy decisions. “The data is not going to be dependable, and it is not going to probably even exist in a lot of cases. So how in the world are they going to actually pull that off with any reasonable confidence in it? Good luck,” said Salisbury. He agreed with my suggestion that the data will also be skewed by comparing recent college graduates with high school leavers well into their careers in their early 30s. In places like Raleigh, North Carolina, which is one of America’s fastest-growing cities, workers with only a high school diploma are in high demand in construction, transportation, and other fields. “You’re right. That’s one of the instances where the data that would be necessary to actually pull off what they conceptually imagine isn’t collected, isn’t available; it’s just no part of the mix,” he stated. Salisbury ended our conversation by echoing what Fansmith, who, when speaking about the complexity of the depleted DoE writing the regulations for the changes to the Parent Plus and GradPlus programmes, said: “Smooth implementation may be too much to hope for, but our guiding star is to avoid an implosion.” “The federal government's infrastructure here is just in total disarray. So there’s not going to be data collected, there's not going to be anything brought forward to be able to pull this off. “There are a bunch of different things in this bill like that they [the government] are operating as if colleges function in a way that colleges actually do not,” said Salisbury. Student healthcare consequences Despite 67% of Americans opposing the proposed US$1 trillion cut to Medicaid, the final version of the OBBB made these cuts – which will impact almost 3.5 million financially disadvantaged post-secondary students who, according to Fansmith, get their healthcare paid for by the federal government programme. Single, able-bodied students will now be required to work 80 hours per month – in a job, through job training, or community service – to maintain their coverage. “Students, often working students already, will now have to balance this requirement,” said Fansmith. “It puts more demands on them and is going to make it harder and harder for them to meet these requirements.” According to Nellums, this new provision will hit students in HBCUs especially hard because of the disproportionate number of students enrolled in these institutions that are also on Medicare. The cuts to Medicare could, also, Fansmith says, result in the closing of rural hospitals because in rural areas, university-run hospitals “tend to be the providers of care”. Cuts to benefits, he explained, become cuts to reimbursements that are available to those health centres. This will put an additional strain on these hospitals’ budgets and could lead to hospital closures – something the governor of Maine, Janet Mills, has already warned about. With a population of only 1.4 million, Maine stands to lose US$4.5 billion and “does not have the financial resources to absorb cuts of this magnitude.” Alternatively, states could choose to increase their contribution, which is presently 36% of Medicare costs. Since all but one state is required to have a balanced budget, politicians will have two choices: the politically unpalatable option of raising taxes or finding the monies elsewhere, which often means cutting grants to public universities. “I suspect that every state is going to end up being in a position where the state itself has to simply raise taxes to make up the difference that the federal government revoked, because the states can't just simply say to all of the people in their state, the hundreds of thousands in Iowa [where Salisbury was when I interviewed him], for example, are going to lose their Medicaid. “So, the state is going to have to increase the amount of money it spends, which means they're going to have to increase taxes, right? And a whole bunch of states have started to talk about this already, like we’re going to have to increase taxes. We simply can't operate like we already want, right?” said Salisbury. According to Fansmith, in the past when faced with similar budgetary crises, states often turned to cutting their grants to the public universities and colleges because, since they charge tuition, they have what’s thought of as an independent revenue stream. Cuts to such major public institutions as the University of Michigan (UM) or the University of California (UCal) system are difficult enough for those institutions and students, though in some cases, UM and UCal, their endowments could help soften the blow. However, for the 50 publicly funded HBCUs, which educate 77% of the total number of HBCU students, state cuts are devastating because these institutions are chronically underfunded as it is. Ivy League endowment tax targets According to Nellums, the reworked endowment tax can be seen as another front in Trump’s battles with Harvard, Columbia, and other Ivy League universities. “We’ve done research that shows that a lot of the institutions that will primarily be impacted by the endowment taxes will be wealthier colleges and universities, such as Ivy League. It seems that the Trump administration is primarily targeting those institutions with the endowment tax.” Two months ago, speaking of their endowments (which in Harvard’s case is more than US$50 billion and in Columbia’s is almost US$15 billion), McMahon all but admitted as much. “It’s billions of dollars that could come into the government if this endowment revenue is taxed. I think the general public will look at that and say that might be a reasonable approach,” she said. The OBBB replaces the endowment tax of 1.4% brought in in 2017, during Trump’s first term, with three tiers; the calculations are based on dividing the endowment by the total student population. Institutions that have an endowment of between US$500,000 and US$750,000 per student will continue to pay 1.4%. Institutions that have an endowment of between US$750,000 and US$2 million will pay the rate of 4%. The rate for institutions with larger endowments is now 8%, a roughly six-fold increase. “For institutions falling into this category,” said Fansmith, “this is a massive increase in the tax they will be paying.” Yale University will now be paying more than US$280 million in taxes on its endowment of US$41billion, said its president, Maurie McInnis , who wrote to the Yale community that, “Taxing universities undermines the education and research that fuel life-saving medical breakthroughs, live-changing innovations, and the economic growth in communities across the country and around the globe.” According to Fansmith, the “net effect of these changes is that about half of institutions that were paying the endowment tax this year won’t have to pay going forward. But those institutions that are paying, in most cases, significantly more than they were paying before”. Increased government control of higher education At the end of our interview, Nellums turned from discussing the impact of the Trump administration’s cuts on critical cancer research, research into dementia, and how universities provide students with the opportunity to succeed and took aim at the Trump administration’s claim that universities are indoctrinating students with left-wing ideology and that they want to bring education back to the states. He told University World News: “What they’re doing is actually increasing the government’s role. They’re trying to have more of a foothold in higher education by also going after the accreditation process. “Make no mistake about it, this [the OBBB] is an attempt to cut funding, but [it is] also an effort to have a stronger hold on what these institutions are doing.”

title: Crisis looming for internationalisation industry in HE
content:
Tweet
University World News has published a variety of articles focusing on internationalisation in the context of recent dramatic geopolitical changes and their impact on higher education globally.
Hans de Wit analysed some of these discussions in his recent article, “What do we mean when we use the word ‘internationalisation’?” But one aspect of this important topic that these discussions have mostly ignored is the business angle of internationalisation.
While Altbach and De Wit wrote “When HE internationalisation operates as an industry” in University World News in April 2023, this trend has intensified in recent years, while at the same time the current geopolitical realities plus the advent and increasing sophistication of AI and related technologies require further analysis of its development and related challenges.
The internationalisation industry is not only big but also very diverse and serves a broad range of needs of the (higher) education sector in an era of increased marketisation and competition. It includes not-for-profit and for-profit entities, serving the public and-or the private good. Without question, internationalisation in its various aspects is now an industry, but, given these challenges, is it an industry in crisis?
Student mobility
The largest segment of the industry is student mobility – with almost seven million students globally mobile, according to UNESCO data for 2023 .
But there are many other, sometimes related, aspects as well. These include branch campuses – there are more than 300 worldwide, and their number is increasing – as well as other forms of transnational education (TNE), franchise operations, articulation programmes, binational universities, and others, mostly aimed at producing income for the partnering institutions.
Stephen Wilkins and Jeroen Huisman identify 11 forms of TNE. In addition, there are many international collaborative research enterprises of all kinds.
No one knows how extensive the internationalisation industry is, but our global estimate is that it is more than US$1.5 trillion annually. A few examples illustrate its size. Student mobility alone produces more than US$40 billion annually for the US economy, £37 billion (US$50 billion) for the United Kingdom, and AU$51 billion (or US$33 billion, where it is the country’s second largest export industry), to name the largest earners.
Countries also devote significant resources to internationalisation. For example, government-funded organisations such as Campus France, the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD), the British Council, NUFFIC in the Netherlands, and EducationUSA and the Fulbright programme in the US are all engaged in the “soft power” of building international student and staff mobility and other programmes, for both political and economic objectives.
It is significant that NUFFIC, the British Council, and especially the Fulbright Program are now subject to severe budget cuts due to changing immigration policies, financial challenges, and populist influences.
These agencies and developments are just the tip of the iceberg of a massive industry that has been developed in the past half-century to serve the increasingly complex internationalisation nexus.
A largely invisible industry
It is not possible to fully describe and analyse this emerging industry. Not only is it too diverse and globally dispersed, but it is also highly opaque, with many players avoiding transparency concerning their activities. And the industry is undergoing significant change, especially in response to rapidly changing geopolitical realities and the increasing importance of artificial intelligence (AI).
The fact that a number of venture capital companies have invested in the industry in the past decade is a strong indication of its importance and potential from a financial perspective. For example, Times Higher Education, in addition to its publication and rankings, is now a data analytics company that builds on the data collected for its rankings as well as being a consultancy and sponsor of conferences and is owned by Inflexion Pvt Equity Partners LLP.
The scope and role of the industry are widespread and diverse and include a variety of consultancies that aid universities with their international programmes, companies that build residences for international students, companies that coordinate with banks to lend tuition funds to students going abroad, ranking companies that provide paid consultancies to help governments and institutions with improving their positions in the rankings and agents that recruit students for institutions that pay them.
Studyportals, as an example, is a Netherlands-based company that provides information on academic institutions and programmes worldwide to prospective students. It also works directly with academic institutions that pay for its services.
Another example of this industry is the recruitment agents. There are thousands of agents globally, with huge numbers in major sending countries, such as China and India.
The American International Recruitment Council, a membership organisation representing the agent community, has 400 institutional members globally and claims to provide ethical standards. The agent industry has come under much criticism for lack of transparency, ethical lapses, and falsifying admissions materials. But it is without doubt a key part of the student mobility ecosphere. Where is the industry heading? This is a period of considerable change, and quite likely crisis, for the internationalisation industry. Geopolitical tensions related to the rise of anti-immigrant and anti-intellectual sentiment combined with housing issues relating to international students in many of the main receiving countries, especially in the Anglosphere, may reshape mobility patterns and will likely reduce total numbers. Transnational education (TNE) operations may become more dominant as an alternative for student mobility, requiring big investments and risk assessments. This includes branch campuses of universities mostly in the Global North, joint degree programmes, franchising arrangements, and other initiatives to retain income and serve students while at the same time reducing international student numbers in the Global North. South-South cooperation and mobility will likely increase – both China and India have ambitious plans – although success is by no means assured. These changes create opportunities for consulting companies and firms involved in placing students in specific programmes. The advent of AI as a tool for selecting places to study and as a means for universities to communicate with prospective students from abroad is already in its early stages and may reshape or even upend the recruitment business. New partnership models may emerge to replace student mobility to fill skilled labour roles in high-income countries, such as tailor-made education schemes in middle- and low-income countries that prepare graduates for jobs abroad, as is already happening in the field of nursing in countries like the Philippines, Tunisia, and Albania. The internationalisation industry faces severe crises – it will no doubt survive so long as there is student mobility and international collaboration globally, and as long as there is a need for skilled labour from the developing world in the rich countries, but it has to adapt to new realities and quality and ethics concerns. title: Plan to withdraw living expenses for foreign PhD students
content:
Tweet
In a bid to boost the sagging number of Japanese doctoral students, the Japanese government is planning to reduce resources for international PhD students. The proposal aims to cut annual living allowances for foreigners, while Japanese students will continue to receive the funding.
The change proposed by a Ministry of Education expert panel made public on 26 June, which is expected to start from April 2026, is against a backdrop where 4,000 of the total 10,564 students in PhD programmes nationwide receiving JPY3 million (US$20,500) each in living expenses, were foreign students, according to the ministry.
Students from China comprised three-quarters of the 39% of PhD students that are international students. Lawmakers claim that many international students fund their living expenses privately.
However, experts have pointed out that weakening aid to foreign students could gravely impact Japanese government plans to attract foreign students and top international professionals to contribute to national employment and research programmes. For example, Japan faces a shortage of almost 750,000 IT engineers by 2040.
Futao Huang, a professor at the Research Institute for Higher Education, Hiroshima University, said the proposal “appears contradictory to Japan’s broader goal of attracting and retaining highly skilled international talent”.
“Cutting living allowances for international doctoral students could discourage talented individuals from choosing Japan, especially when other countries are increasing support to build global research capacity,” Huang said.
Retaining high-performing international graduates could help address skill shortages and strengthen Japan’s position in the global knowledge economy, he added via email.
The proposed change addresses SPRING (Support Pioneering Research Initiated by the Next Generation), implemented in 2021 by the Japan Science and Technology Agency to increase assistance to Japanese students.
It aimed to tackle the domestic decline in PhD enrolment – 2024 domestic PhD enrolment declined 12% compared to a decade ago, while foreigners rose by 35% in the same period, according to official data, which also points out that Japanese students cited financial difficulties and concerns over employment prospects as reasons for not enrolling in PhD programmes.
Political backdrop
Experts also point to the political backdrop behind the proposals. Japanese media reported the SPRING programme came under fire from the ruling conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) in March when it was discussed as part of “excessive reliance on international students and an economic security risk.”
LDP lawmaker Haruko Arimura, referring to limiting foreign students, was quoted in the daily Japan News on March 26 as saying: “without clearly establishing the principle of supporting Japanese students, we cannot gain public understanding”.
“Accepting foreign nationals as immigrants is becoming a major domestic political campaign issue,” pointed out adjunct researcher Kazuyuki Suwa, who teaches Chinese language at Daito Bunka University.
Suwa views the proposal as a blow to Japan’s international profile, referring to Japanese universities as an opportunity to attract foreign students, given the current lower exchange rate for the Japanese currency, the yen, and university tuition fees at JPY 1.2 million annually, considered reasonable by international standards.
Mitsunobu Kano, a professor in the faculty of interdisciplinary science at Okayama University and an expert on the panel advising the ministry on the proposed reforms, explained the change supports the core aim of the SPRING programme – to increase the number of Japanese researchers by providing assistance.
“The programme supports applications from Japanese students, which is the original intention of the Japanese government. There is a critical need to raise the research profile of universities, and aspiring Japanese doctoral students need assistance,” he told University World News.
Kano does not expect a decline in foreign doctoral students in Japan. He noted that top-level students, including foreigners, will continue to receive SPRING research funding as stipulated in the SPRING goals. Financial aid for research – around JPY 400,000 per year – would continue to be available regardless of nationality.
Concern over increase in Chinese students
The increase in the number of Chinese researchers in Japanese universities is also leading to new screening guidelines for foreign doctoral students that became effective in 2022.
While no issues have been made public by officials, policymakers refer to the need to protect against intellectual property theft and cyberattacks, which they see as posing a national threat.
On average, international students are less than 5% of those in tertiary education compared to 20% in the United Kingdom. Japan has set a goal of increasing the low figure to 30% by 2033. The government’s 2023 MIRAI (Mutual Understanding, Intellectual Relations, and Academic Exchange Initiative) Programme – a short-term youth exchange scheme to invite undergraduate and graduate students to Japan – set a goal of achieving 400,000 foreign students by 2033, including increasing international doctorate students to 33% from the current 21%. The policy also aims to increase foreign graduate employment to 60% from the current 48% that includes vocational students.

title: Can Asia become a ‘sanctuary’ for global student talent?
content:
Tweet
Universities in Asia are putting out the welcome mat to international students looking for alternatives due to the current uncertainty over student visas to the United States and other policies affecting international students at American universities.
While some countries in Asia have announced funding to attract researchers and faculty members who wish to leave the US, whether they are American or foreign academics, others have focused on streamlining procedures for students who wish to transfer from the US mid-programme.
Singapore
This week Singapore joined several other Asian countries in saying its door is open as a ‘sanctuary’ for global talent.
Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs Vivian Balakrishnan, in a speech at the 120th anniversary celebrations of the National University of Singapore (NUS), said: “If we can maintain the confidence and the ability to be independent, to be open, to be inclusive, to be scientific, to be rational, and to be able to work with people regardless of where they have come from, regardless of provenance, we can make Singapore, and especially NUS, a sanctuary for global talent who actually just want to do research, innovate, and apply to make the world a better place.”
He pointed to increased geopolitical tensions, such as the rivalries between superpowers, which have been accelerated by technological advancements.
Dr Balakrishnan, an NUS alumnus and a former president of the NUS Students’ Union, said on 3 July: “NUS needs to have open gates, and we need to have our fair share of access to talent and ideas, while still remembering that this is the citadel based in Singapore, to protect Singapore, dependent on the hard core of Singaporeans, but never with closed minds or closed attitudes.”
But some academics saw the message as somewhat mixed.
Ja Ian Chong, associate professor in the department of political science at NUS, said “whether or how Singapore universities may or may not be more open to foreign students is unclear from the speech”, pointing out that Balakrishnan is minister for foreign affairs, not education.
“The degree to which his speech marks a direction for higher education policy is uncertain,” he told University World News.
The call for openness contrasts with recent moves by Singapore to reverse a policy of attracting high numbers of foreign students under its previous ‘Global Schoolhouse’ scheme to make Singapore an international education hub.
The change in policy included a highly controversial move in 2021 to close down Yale-NUS college , which had been set up to attract international students.
Some academics were looking for clues in the minister’s speech for signals Singapore will be more open to international students again.
NUS College, with a stronger focus on Singaporean students, has replaced the now shuttered Yale-NUS College at NUS.
This year the new college said it received a record 10,000 applications for its liberal arts degrees for its 400 places. In 2022, when it first opened, amid negative publicity over the closure of Yale-NUS, it received 7,000 applications.
According to Singapore’s Immigration and Checkpoints Authority, there are 73,000 foreign student pass holders in the city-state.
The government does not provide a breakdown by nationality, but estimates put the number of students from China at half the total, including some with graduate degrees from the US coming to Singapore for graduate study.
Meanwhile, a report titled 2024 Blue Paper for Chinese Overseas Students Returning to China for Employment released in March by the Chinese Service Centre for Scholarly Exchange under China’s Ministry of Education noted that Singapore now ranks second among preferred study abroad destinations for Chinese students, overtaking the US for the first time.
Rather than students, Balakrishnan’s speech “seems to me more like an effort to attract academic talent to Singapore. The degree to which that can be done without a more open environment is less apparent to me”, said Chong Ja, referring to academic freedom concerns in Singapore .
“Note that Balakrishnan also describes the university as a citadel, albeit with open gates. A place with high walls and fixed entryways seems to sit uneasily with a call for the openness and inclusivity that supports true innovation and intellectual breakthroughs,” Chong Ja added.
Another Singaporean academic, speaking on condition of anonymity, told University World News: “Singapore is less interested in opening up to more students from abroad but wants its pick of international researchers who may be worried about the (visa) situation at Harvard, particularly researchers in areas that align with its own strategic science and technology priorities, including high-end technologies.”
He added: “Hong Kong has stolen a march on Singapore in presenting itself as a sanctuary for those leaving the US, and Singapore wants to say it is also open for transfers, but in a limited way.” Hong Kong Hong Kong was first off the mark to announce it was open to applicants from Harvard University and others affected by US visa policies. On 23 May, the day after the Trump administration’s announcement that it was revoking Harvard University’s right to admit foreign students – a move the university is fighting – HKUST issued an “open invitation” to international undergraduate and postgraduate students currently enrolled at Harvard University, as well as those holding confirmed offers for Harvard degree programmes, to continue their academic pursuits at HKUST. Hong Kong’s Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu, whose role includes chancellor of Hong Kong’s public universities, said on 27 May: “Hong Kong will welcome any students who have been discriminated against by the US policy, who face difficulties studying, or continuing their studies in US universities.” In late June the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) announced it had received nearly 200 enquiries from students worldwide – a 40% increase year-on-year, since 2023. The university administration said it sent admission offers to six students “who either hold Harvard acceptance letters or are currently on postgraduate programmes at Harvard”. Six of these had accepted places at HKUST by 24 June; five of them were postgraduate students from mainland China, Pakistan, and Georgia who were offered scholarships by HKUST. “HKUST is firmly dedicated to establishing Hong Kong as the premier destination for the world’s brightest minds,” said Professor Emily Nason, director of undergraduate recruitment and admissions at HKUST. HKUST also pointed to a record number of applicants for the 2025-26 academic year, with nearly 20,000 undergraduate applications from outside Hong Kong for around 800 places – more than double its total undergraduate enrolment. Xiang Zhang, president of the University of Hong Kong (HKU), said last month it had received about 300 enquiries from affected US students and made “multiple offers”, without providing details. The Hong Kong government announced. On 27 June its eight publicly funded universities had received around 850 transfer enquiries related to “sudden policy changes”, particularly in the US. Uncertainty Uncertainty dogs those applying for visas to the US, while international students and researchers already in the US fear for their future after US President Trump said international students at Harvard University must either transfer to another university or leave the country. Students in Hong Kong and China reported a halt to visa appointments at that time, while students in other countries reported delays. Balakrishnan referred to this during a visit to Washington, DC last month, stressing that though US policies were not specifically directed at Singapore but all international students in the US, a country like Singapore can “become affected as collateral damage… and there will be some uncertainty.” “Nevertheless, we will continue to pursue this with the American authorities, and I hope we will be able to find suitable solutions for our students who want to pursue educational opportunities in the United States,” he said in remarks to the media during his 4 to 7 June visit to the US. At a 7 June media briefing , he said with regard to Singaporean students at Harvard: “We are also trying to find solutions to deal with the worst-case scenario where they would not be able to physically study in Boston, and we have got some ideas for how we can help them.” Balakrishnan added: “For others who are not yet here, or who have not yet secured visas – you may also need to have backup plans.” South Korea Other countries in Asia have announced plans for students and researchers. South Korea’s prestigious Yonsei University announced on 3 July it had set up a new transfer system to accept transfers from international undergraduates in the middle of the academic year with a continuous undergraduate transfer admissions process for foreign nationals and overseas Koreans beginning in the first semester of 2026 for students who faced sudden visa or legal difficulties in the US. Overseas Koreans and international students in their second or third years of study will be eligible regardless of the country they are studying in and can transfer to South Korea after completing screening for academic requirements, subject-specific exams, and interviews. Yonsei University said it is also working on arrangements with top American universities to allow students to temporarily study in Seoul while receiving credits toward their home institution's degree. According to a Yonsei University statement on 3 July, the special transfer program was a response to the US’ strengthened visa screening and “growing legal conflicts between universities” and the US administration – referring to Harvard and other institutions. Describing its scheme as “the most rapid, specific, and effective response” among South Korean universities, the statement read: “This measure reflects the reality that a sharp increase in students have had their studies abroad interrupted due to the US government's recent strengthened social media screening, entry restrictions on certain countries, and university-specific measures to revoke the right to accept international students. “We will do our best and offer institutional and financial support to help talented students around the world continue their studies at Yonsei University,” said Yoon Dong-sup, the university’s president. “Yonsei will continue to strengthen its role as a global education and research hub. Yonsei University aims to go beyond simple crisis response and practice the social responsibility that educational institutions must fulfil in the face of an international higher education crisis,” the statement noted. Seoul National University also unveiled new measures aimed at international talent, expanding eligibility for its international joint research support programme, which previously served only graduate students. The university also launched a new fellowship programme since March to recruit international postdoctoral researchers. Korea University on 1 July said it had finalised changes to its academic regulations to allow mid-year transfers. “We plan to actively recruit researchers from elite institutions like Harvard to enhance our global research competitiveness,” a university official told local media. Japan Japan in mid-June said it had allocated around US$700 million in an emergency package to attract talented researchers to Japan “amid an exodus of talent from the United States”, notably surpassing the €500 million (US$580 million) measure announced by the European Union in May. “We will make utmost efforts to make our country the most attractive in the world for researchers,” said Minister of State for Science and Technology Policy Minoru Kiuchi at a press conference on 16 June. The initiative highlighted “expanding the strategic hiring of excellent overseas researchers, including Japanese living overseas, as soon as possible, with an eye to the new autumn semester”. The Japanese government aims to hire administrative staff fluent in foreign languages and strengthen support for families accompanying researchers. At a meeting of the Council for Science, Technology and Innovation chaired by Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba on 4 June, Ishiba instructed relevant ministries to recruit researchers seeking to leave the US. Individual universities in Japan are also seeking to attract researchers. At least 87 Japanese universities have earmarked new budgets to host foreign researchers. Among them are top national institutions such as the University of Tokyo, Kyoto University, and Tohoku University, which lead Japan’s world-class scientific and technological research.

title: Trump administration asks commission to decertify Harvard
content:
Tweet
The United States government recently turned the screw two more times against Harvard University by announcing it was subpoenaing the university’s international student disciplinary records and by asking the New England Commission of Higher Education (NECHE) to decertify the university founded in 1636.
The administration claims that these actions, as well as a number of others, including the freezing of more than US$2 billion in research grants and contracts and the freezing of Harvard’s ability to enrol international students, are necessary to bring the university to heel over its allowing antisemitism to fester on campus and its being “a wilful participant in antisemitic harassment of Jewish students, faculty, and staff”, during the pro-Palestinian protests following the start of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2022 – a charge that Harvard has contested in court.
‘Allegations of disciplinary disparity’
The subpoena is the latest step in the government’s investigation of “allegations of disciplinary disparity involving nonimmigrant students”, that is, that Harvard did not discipline students accused of antisemitic acts dating back to 1 January 2020.
In announcing the subpoena, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) used the same pugilistic tone that President Donald J Trump did only a few hours later when he addressed the subpoena by saying : “Harvard Bad – totally antisemitic.”
“We tried to do things the easy way with Harvard. Now, through their refusal to cooperate, we have to do things the hard way. Harvard, like other universities, has allowed foreign students to abuse their visa privileges and advocate for violence and terrorism on campus.
“If Harvard won’t defend the interests of its students, then we will,” DHS Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin stated .
As it has in regard to numerous investigations and executive orders, Harvard spokesperson John Newton said the university would “comply with all lawful requests and obligations”, as it had when it handed over some disciplinary records a few months ago, but it “remains unwavering in its efforts to protect its community and core principles against unfounded retribution by the federal government”.
Revoking Harvard’s accreditation
Earlier in the day, Secretary of Education Linda McMahon published a letter to the NECHE calling on it to revoke Harvard’s accreditation, which would financially undermine the university because it would bar it both from receiving research grants and enrolling students on federal financial aid; roughly 20% of Harvard’s 6,700 undergraduates receive Pell Grants, monies available to the nation’s poorest students.
McMahon’s letter tied Harvard’s (admitted) antisemitic problem both to its “obligation to students, educators and the American taxpayer” and to its failure to “preserve academic integrity and a campus culture conducive to truth-seeking and learning”.
Because many of the research grants made to Harvard that have been cut were for medical research and were funded by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), its director, Robert F Kennedy Jr, co-signed the letter.
In the statement issued by McMahon’s office, Kennedy, who, like his father, Senator (New York) Robert F Kennedy, and uncle, President John F Kennedy, graduated from Harvard, excoriated his alma mater: “When an institution – no matter how prestigious – abandons its mission and fails to protect its students, it forfeits the legitimacy that accreditation is designed to uphold.
“HHS and the Department of Education will actively hold Harvard accountable through sustained oversight until it restores public trust and ensures a campus free of discrimination.”

title: Medical education scam busted, involves high officials
content:
Tweet
In a sweeping operation that has shaken India’s medical education sector, the country’s premier investigation agency, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), has unearthed what is believed to be one of the largest medical education corruption cases in the country’s history.
The scheme allegedly involved what the agency called “egregious” acts, including bribery, criminal conspiracy, and forgery, as well as collusion.
In some cases, fictitious faculty and patients were presented to create an illusion of compliance during inspections.
According to the CBI, the sprawling case involves a complex web of collusion among officials from the Health Ministry, the National Medical Commission (NMC), intermediaries, and representatives from private medical colleges, all allegedly engaged in corrupt activities to ensure favourable inspection reports for medical institutions.
The CBI probe has reportedly implicated a wide array of public officials, private entities, and institution leaders nationwide, facing charges that include bribery, conspiracy, breach of official secrecy, and forgery.
The scope of the alleged scam spans multiple states, suggesting a coordinated effort that has ramifications for over 40 institutions nationwide and undermines the integrity of medical education across India, experts said.
The NMC is a regulatory authority in India responsible for overseeing medical education, professionals, institutions, and research. It recognises medical qualifications, accredits medical colleges, registers medical practitioners, and monitors medical practices while assessing the medical infrastructure across the country.
FIR names 34 people
On 7 July, CBI filed a First Information Report, or FIR (first formal record of a crime), naming 34 persons, including senior officials from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), the NMC, and various private institutions. It included a former chairman of the higher education regulatory body, the University Grants Commission (UGC).
According to a CBI official not authorised to speak publicly, the alleged conspiracy revolves around the unauthorised leak of sensitive regulatory information, manipulation of mandatory inspection processes, and large-scale bribery aimed at securing favourable treatment for private medical colleges.
Recently, the CBI apprehended eight persons, among them three doctors from the NMC, alleged to have accepted a bribe of INR5.5 million (about US$64,700) to furnish a favourable inspection report for the Rawatpura Institute of Medical Sciences and Research located in Naya Raipur, in the central state of Chhattisgarh.
The FIR alleges the heart of the scam lies within the Ministry of Health, where a cadre of officials orchestrated a complex plan that enabled unauthorised access to confidential files and sensitive information in exchange for substantial payments.
At least eight officials from the Ministry of Health have been accused of allegedly leaking internal documents and facilitating bribe transactions. These officials reportedly manipulated inspection teams and altered documentation to secure favourable outcomes.
“The modus operandi included manipulated digital records. Digitalisation was supposed to bring transparency, but it was manipulated too.
Fake attendance, fake patient records, all digitised fraudulently,” said Amulya Nidhi, national co-convenor of the People’s Health Movement of India , a network of civil society organisations and academic institutions, told University World News. “This isn’t just a scam; it’s an institutional collapse,” said Nidhi. “Regulators have become brokers. The very people entrusted with safeguarding India’s medical future are selling it off.” Colleges gained access to sensitive data Several officials, in partnership with intermediaries, provided critical information about statutory inspections to select medical colleges, according to the investigation. The CBI’s findings provide a clear illustration of regulatory capture. This included advance notification of inspection dates and the identities of assessors, allowing these institutions to create fraudulent setups that would pass regulatory evaluations. Evidence includes ‘ghost’ faculty, falsified biometric attendance, and inflated patient numbers. The CBI’s findings suggest that prior access to sensitive data through the network afforded these colleges considerable leverage, enabling them to engineer arrangements, such as bribing assessors, employing fictitious faculty, and falsifying patient admissions during inspections. The agency has traced hefty bribes exchanged among NMC teams, intermediaries, and college representatives, often funnelled through hawala – a non-formal cash transfer system that is illegal in India – networks. Arrests As the investigation unfolds, CBI has already made several arrests and is in the process of tracking the flow of illicit funds while scrutinising the involvement of prominent persons, including a former UGC chairman, Professor Dhirendra Pal Singh, currently chancellor of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai. Noteworthy figures implicated in the scandal include Ravi Shankar Maharaj, a controversial ‘godman’ or spiritual leader and Chairman of Shri Rawatpura Sarkar Institute of Medical Sciences and Research, and Suresh Singh Bhadoria, chairman of Indore’s Index Medical College. Other prominent names alleged to be involved include Mayur Raval, Registrar of Gitanjali University in Udaipur, Rajasthan, and Jitu Lal Meena, a key intermediary with connections to both regulators and college owners. The scale of the bribes reportedly reached several million rupees. The CBI has executed raids across multiple states, targeting over 40 locations, signalling that the investigation is far from complete. CBI indicated this is just the beginning, suggesting more arrests are imminent as evidence is examined and financial trails pursued. Just the beginning As the investigation expands, there is increasing pressure on the NMC and Health Ministry to overhaul their inspection and approval processes. “Even though FIRs were filed under the Prevention of Corruption Act and Indian Penal Code, NMC didn’t cancel licenses of involved colleges or doctors. If ethical education isn’t happening, those colleges must be shut down. Otherwise, we are producing unethical doctors who will practice fraudulently,” Nidhi said. Medical education experts and academics are calling for a total overhaul of the inspection process. This issue has persisted for years, but this time the CBI possesses undeniable evidence, said a senior doctor in Delhi, who wished to remain anonymous. The ongoing investigation represents a concerted effort to restore integrity within the medical education sector, he added. Nidhi said: “The entire scam has exposed the failure of private medical education in India. Approvals are now being auctioned like vegetables in a market. This touches everything – ethics, education, healthcare, and social work – and has completely shaken public trust.” He added: “If you graduate unethical doctors, you breed unethical practice. You’re laying the foundation for systemic fraud. People who believed in India’s healthcare system feel utterly betrayed.”
